newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan leader ready to visit Central, South America.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan leader ready to visit Central, South America.

text.p: Taiwan announced on Wednesday that President Lee Teng-hui would visit four diplomatic allies in Central and South America next month, a trip seen as the latest round in a long diplomatic tussle between Taipei and Beijing.
"President Lee ... will visit Panama, Honduras, El Salvador and Paraguay in his forthcoming trip," Foreign Minister John Chang said in a news conference.
Lee will leave Taipei on September 4 and return on September 19, Chang said.

He said Lee was invited by Panama to attend a global conference on the Panama Canal on September 7. Lee would head to Honduras on September 9 and go to El Salvador on September 11 to attend a Central American leaders' summit.
The president would visit Paraguay in South America on September 14-17 before returning to Taipei, Chang said.
Foreign ministry officials said Lee will make transit stops at Hawaii on September 4-5 and September 17-18.
The United States has agreed to issue a transit visa for Lee, despite China's warning that it would hurt Sino-U.S. ties.

The announcement came a day after Taiwan scored a modest victory in an almost five-decade diplomatic tug-of-war with Beijing through resumption of diplomatic relations with the Central Afrian nation of Chad.
But local media said Saint Lucia, a Taiwanese ally in the Caribbean, is mulling switching ties to Beijing.
To sabotage Taiwan's foreign ties, Beijing has stepped up efforts to increase its influence in Latin America, where Taiwan has 15 diplomatic allies.

Beijing, which regards Taiwan as a renegade province since the end of a civil war in 1949, has said Taiwan is not entitled to international relations and other countries should not permit visits by high-level officials from the island.
The rivals have competed aggressively for diplomatic recognition, often accusing each other of using large sums of cash and aid to woo potential allies.
Taiwan now maintains official ties with 31 countries, though that number would fall to 30 when South Africa, Taiwan's biggest ally, switches recognition to Beijing at the end of 1997.
Analysts say China can easily assert its influence in Latin America, now that its foreign exchange reserves have risen to more than US$100 billion.
Shortly after Chang visited Saint Lucia in July, Beijing offered US$1 million in educational aid to the Caribbean island.

The local United Evening News said China had asked Saint Lucia to consider switching official recognition to Beijing, and the Caribbean country was expected to discuss the issue during a cabinet meeting on August 14.
Taiwan's foreign ministry on Wednesday declined comment on the report, saying relations with Saint Lucia were firm.
A western diplomat in Taiwan said after the loss of Chad, Beijing would certainly make greater efforts to woo Saint Lucia and other diplomatic allies of Taiwan in the Americas.
"Not many can resist the potentially huge profits in the vast mainland market and the attractive aid from China," the diplomatic said on condition of annoymity.
